processing: A green tea made by spreading the fresh leaf, fixing, rolling, pan-firing and shaping. Local accounts stress that some key stages still resist full mechanisation.
harvest_season: No exact picking dates are recorded; as with other Hubei greens, spring is the usual and most valued picking.
appearance_dry: Little is recorded; typical of shaped Hubei greens, expect tidy, dark green leaf.
appearance_liquor: Clear, bright green, taking on a slight yellow tint in the second steep.
appearance_wet: Typical of spring green tea: tender, fresh green buds and leaves.
taste_profile: Mellow and sweet with a scent like cooked chestnut that peaks around the second steep, and a lasting sweet return.

brewing.notes: A general starting point for this class. The chestnut note is said to be strongest in the second steep, so do not judge it on the first.

vintage_note: As with other Chinese greens, it is sold as the current year's spring harvest, with earlier pickings usually priced higher. There is no ageing market. Look for the geographical indication, the Wujiatai or Xuan'en origin and a picking date.
description:
Wujiatai Gong Cha is a green tea from Wujiatai village in Wanzhai township, Xuan'en county, in the Enshi prefecture of western Hubei. Gong means tribute, and the name leans on a local story about a Qing emperor. It holds national geographical indication status.

The making is a careful version of the green tea routine: spread, fix, roll, pan-fire, shape. The heat work is probably where its best-known trait comes from, since a chestnut scent is common in well pan-fired greens, though no account spells out that link for this tea.

Descriptions follow it steep by steep: clear green and mellow at first, a stronger chestnut aroma and a touch of yellow in the second, then a bright, fragrant third. Water that is too hot flattens it quickly.

Buy the current spring and check the origin, since a tribute name is easy to borrow. The village has large organic-certified gardens, which is worth asking about but is no guarantee of a good cup.
history:
The local account dates its fame to 1784, the 49th year of the Qianlong reign, when the tea is said to have gone to court. The emperor is said to have praised it and sent a plaque inscribed 皇恩宠锡 to the producer Wu Changchen. This story comes from local and news retellings, and it should be read as tradition.

In recent decades the name has become a regional brand with formal protection and a substantial organic planting in the village.
